story.title: Microsoft says AI agents are like insider threats as ‘frontier models can’t be trusted’

facts.text: Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak.

Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them.
Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies .
The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch.
“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote , adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable.
They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”
Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways.

In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw.
It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task.
That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.

But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.”
Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents.
The launch comes as Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents.
The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both.
OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models.
Earlier this month, in his private blog , Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products.
He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch.
But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound.
The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit.

This idea of agents as untrustworthy insiders is taking hold across the broader industry, too.
